content: 1. The mosquito will simultaneously come into contact with insecticides in a mosaic strategy designed to mitigate resistance. This involves applying insecticides with different modes of action in separate parts of a covered area, often in a grid pattern, so that different segments of the mosquito population are exposed to different insecticides. 2. Mosquitoes can develop resistance to insecticides, which is their ability to survive exposure to a standard dose. This resistance may arise from physiological or behavioral adaptations. 3. Insecticide rotation is a strategy where insecticides with different modes of action are applied sequentially to delay or reduce the development of resistance. 4. Insecticide tolerance refers to a less-than-average susceptibility to insecticides, but it is not inherited as resistance. 5. Contact insecticides are toxic substances that act on mosquitoes when they rest on treated surfaces. The insecticide is absorbed through their tarsi (feet). 6. Fumigant insecticides release vapor from a volatile substance to exert their toxic effects. 7. Residual insecticides, when applied to a surface, maintain their insecticidal activity for an extended period through either contact or fumigant action. 8. Integrated Vector Management (IVM) is a rational decision-making process aimed at optimizing the use of resources for vector control. 9. Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in school-aged children involves administering a full course of antimalarial medicine at predefined intervals to prevent illness in areas with moderate to high malaria transmission. 10. Intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi) is synonymous with perennial malaria chemoprevention. 11. Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) involves giving pregnant women a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medicine during routine prenatal visits, regardless of whether they are infected with malaria. 12. Invasive species are non-native organisms that establish themselves in a new ecosystem and cause, or have the potential to cause, harm to the environment, economy, or human health. 13. Larval source management involves controlling aquatic habitats that serve as potential breeding grounds for mosquito larvae to prevent the completion of their immature stages. 14. Larvicides are substances used to kill mosquito larvae. 15. The latent period in Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale infections refers to the asymptomatic interval between the primary infection and subsequent relapses, during which parasites are absent from the bloodstream but present in liver cells (hepatocytes). 16. Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are factory-treated mosquito nets made of material with insecticide incorporated or bound to the fibers. These nets must retain effective biological activity for at least 20 WHO-standard washes under laboratory conditions and three years of recommended use in the field. 17. Malaria control refers to the reduction of disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, or mortality to a locally acceptable level through deliberate efforts. Continued interventions are necessary to sustain control. 18. Malaria elimination is the interruption of local transmission, reducing the incidence of indigenous cases to zero in a defined geographical area through deliberate activities. Continued measures are required to prevent re-establishment of transmission. 19. Malaria eradication is the permanent reduction to zero of the worldwide incidence of infection caused by human malaria parasites through deliberate activities. Once eradication is achieved, interventions are no longer required. 20. Malaria infection is the presence of Plasmodium parasites in blood or tissues, confirmed by diagnostic testing. 21. The malaria mortality rate is the number of deaths from malaria per unit of population during a defined period. 22. Malaria pigment (hemozoin) is a brown-to-black granular material formed by malaria parasites as a by-product of hemoglobin digestion. It is visible in mature trophozoites and schizonts and may also be phagocytosed by monocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils. 23. Malaria prevalence (or parasite prevalence) is the proportion of a specified population with malaria infection at a given time. 24. Malaria rebound refers to an increase in malaria incidence following a temporary reduction in transmission due to effective interventions, such as chemoprevention, vaccination, or vector control, when the population becomes exposed to higher transmission levels. 25. Malaria receptivity is the degree to which an ecosystem in a given area at a given time allows for the transmission of Plasmodium species from one human to another via a mosquito vector. 26. Malaria reintroduction occurs when introduced cases (first-generation local transmission cases epidemiologically linked to a confirmed imported case) appear in a country or area where the disease had previously been eliminated. 27. Malaria risk stratification involves classifying geographical areas or localities based on factors that determine receptivity and vulnerability to malaria transmission. 28. Malaria stratification is the classification of geographical areas or localities based on epidemiological, ecological, social, and economic determinants to guide malaria interventions. 29. Cross-border malaria refers to malaria transmission associated with the movement of individuals or mosquitoes across borders. 30. A malaria-free area is one where there is no ongoing local mosquito-borne malaria transmission, and the risk of acquiring malaria is limited to infection from introduced cases. 31. Malarial potential refers to the potential level of transmission in a given area, arising from the combination of malaria receptivity, the importation rate of malaria parasites, and infectivity. 32. A malariometric survey is conducted in a representative sample of selected age groups to estimate malaria prevalence and the coverage of interventions. 33. A malarious area is one where malaria transmission is occurring or has occurred within the preceding three years. 34. Mass drug administration (MDA) involves administering a full treatment course of an antimalarial to all age groups in a defined geographical area, except those for whom the medicine is contraindicated, at approximately the same time and often at repeated intervals. 35. Mass screening is a population-wide assessment of risk factors for malaria infection to identify subgroups for further intervention, such as diagnostic testing, treatment, or preventive services. 36. Mass screening, testing, and treatment involve screening an entire population for risk factors, testing individuals at risk, and treating those with a positive test result. 37. Mass testing and focal drug administration involve testing a population and treating groups of individuals or entire households in which one or more infections are detected. 38. Mass testing and treatment involve parasitological screening of the entire population of a delimited geographical area and treating those with a positive test result at approximately the same time. 39. Medicine safety refers to the characteristics of a medicine that reflect its potential to cause harm, including important identified risks and potential risks associated with the drug. 40. Merozoites are the extracellular stage of a parasite released into host plasma when a hepatic or erythrocytic schizont ruptures. These merozoites can then invade red blood cells. 41. Moderate to high perennial transmission refers to persistent Plasmodium falciparum transmission at rates resulting in a parasite prevalence greater than 10% or an annual parasite incidence greater than 250 per 1,000. 42. Monotherapy is antimalarial treatment with a single active compound or a synergistic combination of two compounds with related mechanisms of action. 43. A national focus register is a centralized database of all malaria infection foci in a country, including relevant data on physical geography, parasites, hosts, and vectors for each focus. 44. A national malaria case register is a centralized database with individual records of all malaria cases registered in a country. 45. Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) are mosquito nets that repel, disable, or kill mosquitoes that come into contact with the insecticide on the netting material. ITNs include those requiring treatment and retreatment (conventional nets) and long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs). 46. An oocyst is the stage of the malaria parasite that develops from the ookinete and grows on the outer wall of the midgut of the female mosquito. 47. The oocyst rate is the percentage of female Anopheles mosquitoes with oocysts on their midgut. 48. An ookinete is the motile stage of the malaria parasite following fertilization of the macrogamete and preceding oocyst formation. 49. Parasitaemia refers to the presence of parasites in the blood. 50. Asymptomatic parasitaemia is the presence of asexual parasites in the blood without symptoms of illness. 51. Parasite clearance time is the time between the first drug administration and the first examination in which no parasites are present in the blood by microscopy. 52. Parasite density is the number of asexual parasites per unit volume of blood or per number of red blood cells. 53. Low parasite density refers to the presence of Plasmodium parasites in the blood at a density below 100 parasites/μL. 54. The patent period is the duration during which malaria parasitaemia is detectable. 55. Perennial malaria chemoprevention involves administering a full treatment course of an antimalarial medicine at predefined intervals to children at risk of severe malaria to prevent illness in moderate to high perennial malaria transmission settings. 56. Plasmodium is a genus of protozoan blood parasites of vertebrates that includes the causal agents of malaria. P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. vivax cause malaria in humans. Human infection with the monkey malaria parasite P. knowlesi and occasionally other simian malaria species may occur in tropical forest areas. 57. Post-discharge malaria chemoprevention involves administering a full treatment course of an antimalarial medicine to children hospitalized for severe anemia, starting at the time of hospital discharge and continuing at predefined intervals. 58. Pre-erythrocytic development refers to the development of the malaria parasite from the time it first enters the host and invades liver cells until the hepatic schizont ruptures. 59. The pre-patent period is the time between inoculation of parasites and the first appearance of parasitaemia. 60. Prequalification is the process of ensuring that health products are safe, appropriate, and meet stringent quality standards for international procurement. 61. Preventive chemotherapy involves using medicines, either alone or in combination, to prevent malaria infections and their consequences. 62. Prophylaxis refers to any method of protection from or prevention of disease. When applied to chemotherapy, it is commonly termed chemoprophylaxis. 63. Causal prophylaxis is the complete prevention of erythrocytic infection by destroying the pre-erythrocytic forms of the parasite. 64. A rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is an immunochromatographic lateral flow device for the rapid detection of malaria parasite antigens. 65. A combination rapid diagnostic test can detect multiple malaria species. 66. The rapid diagnostic test positivity rate is the proportion of positive results among all rapid diagnostic tests performed. 67. Reactive case detection and treatment involve parasitological screening of every person living with or near a person with a confirmed malaria case and/or every person likely exposed to infection at the same time and place as the index case, followed by treatment of those with a positive test result. 68. Reactive drug administration involves administering a full treatment course of an antimalarial medicine as chemoprevention to every person living with or near a person with a confirmed malaria infection and/or to every person likely exposed to infection at the same time and place as the index case. 69. Reactive indoor residual spraying involves applying residual insecticide to the interior surfaces of dwellings in the location of the index case and neighboring houses at approximately the same time. 70. Receptivity refers to the susceptibility of an ecosystem to malaria transmission. 71. Recrudescence is the recurrence of asexual parasitaemia of the same genotype(s) that caused the original illness due to incomplete clearance of asexual parasites after antimalarial treatment. 72. Recurrence is the reappearance of asexual parasitaemia after treatment, which may be due to recrudescence, relapse (in P. vivax and P. ovale infections only), or a new infection. 73. Reinfection is a new infection that follows a primary infection. It can be distinguished from recrudescence by the parasite genotype, which is often (but not always) different from that of the initial infection. 74. Reintroduction risk is the risk that endemic malaria will be re-established in a specific area after its elimination. 75. Relapse is the recurrence of asexual parasitaemia in P. vivax or P. ovale infections arising from hypnozoites. 76. A repellent is any substance that causes avoidance in mosquitoes, particularly substances that deter them from settling on the skin of the host (topical repellent) or entering an area or room (area repellent, spatial repellent, or excito-repellent). 77. Resistance refers to the ability of a parasite or vector to survive exposure to a drug or insecticide that would normally be effective. 78. A ring form (or ring-stage trophozoite) is a young, usually ring-shaped malaria trophozoite before pigment is evident by microscopy. 79. A schizont is a stage of the malaria parasite in host liver cells (hepatic schizont) or red blood cells (erythrocytic schizont) that undergoes nuclear division by schizogony, resulting in multiple nuclei. 80. Screening involves identifying groups at risk that may require further intervention, such as diagnostic testing, treatment, or preventive services. 81. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention involves the intermittent administration of full treatment courses of an antimalarial medicine to children at risk of severe malaria to prevent malarial illness in areas with seasonal malaria. The objective is to maintain therapeutic concentrations of an antimalarial drug in the blood throughout the period of greatest malaria risk. 82. A six-month spraying cycle involves repeating insecticide spraying after a six-month interval. 83. Spraying frequency refers to the number of regular applications of insecticide per house per year, usually through indoor residual spraying. 84. Spraying interval is the time between successive applications of insecticide. 85. Focal spraying involves spray coverage by indoor residual spraying and/or space spraying of houses or habitats in a limited geographical area. 86. Residual spraying (IRS) involves spraying the interior walls and ceilings of dwellings with a residual insecticide to kill or repel endophilic mosquito vectors of malaria. 87. Surveillance is the continuous, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of disease-specific data.
